cues.speaker: KE
cues.text: Mmm. Let's think. So your methodology would involve the children recording what they eat.

cues.speaker: KE
cues.text: OK, but you'd also need to have access to the children's medical records and I don't

cues.speaker: KE
cues.text: think people would be happy about that; confidentiality would be an issue.

cues.speaker: KE
cues.text: If you could get the right data, the conclusions might be significant, but I suspect it's

cues.speaker: KE
cues.text: just not going to be easy.

cues.speaker: KE
cues.text: Have you thought about doing an experiment using animals?

cues.speaker: KE
cues.text: Well, the animals don't have to be harmed in any way.

cues.speaker: KE
cues.text: It could just be an experiment where they're given a certain diet and the effects are

cues.speaker: KE
cues.text: observed.

cues.speaker: KE
cues.text: Yes, you'd have to submit an outline of the experiment and fill in a form, but it's quite

cues.speaker: KE
cues.text: straightforward.

cues.speaker: RE
cues.text: But if we found out that, say, a particular diet affects the health of animals, the same

cues.speaker: RE
cues.text: thing wouldn't necessarily be true for people, would it?

cues.speaker: KE
cues.text: No that's true, but the findings for any experiment are going to be limited.

cues.speaker: KE
cues.text: It's inevitable.

cues.speaker: RE
cues.text: I suppose so. So what animals could I use to investigate the effects of diet? Mice?

cues.speaker: KE
cues.text: Yes. You'd need experimental mice – ones that have been specially bred for experiments.

cues.speaker: KE
cues.text: OK, so what will your experiment be investigating exactly?

cues.speaker: RE
cues.text: Well, something to do with nutrition. So maybe we could look at food supplements...

cues.speaker: RE
cues.text: things like extra iron and extra protein, and their impact on health.

cues.speaker: KE
cues.text: Mmm. That might be rather broad.

cues.speaker: KE
cues.text: Maybe just look at the effects of one supplement, like sugar, on the health of the mice?

cues.speaker: RE
cues.text: In fact, maybe the focus could be on whether mice can control their own diet.

cues.speaker: KE
cues.text: So, what happens when they have access to more sugar, that they don't really need?

cues.speaker: RE
cues.text: Exactly. Do they eat it or do they decide to leave it?

cues.speaker: KE
cues.text: Great. Then later on, you could do a follow-up experiment adding another variable.

cues.speaker: KE
cues.text: Like, you could give some of the mice the chance to be more active, running on a wheel or

cues.speaker: KE
cues.text: something, and the others just sit around and don't do much.

cues.speaker: RE
cues.text: Or I could repeat the experiment but change the type of food I provided . . .

cues.speaker: RE
cues.text: or use mice with a different genetic structure.

cues.speaker: RE
cues.text: But I think your idea would be more interesting, I might think about that some more.

cues.speaker: RE
cues.text: So can I talk through a possible procedure for the experiment where mice are given a

cues.speaker: RE
cues.text: sugar supplement?

cues.speaker: KE
cues.text: Sure. I did a similar experiment in college actually.

cues.speaker: KE
cues.text: I'd say about 12. And all young ones, not a mixture of old and young.

cues.speaker: RE
cues.text: OK. And I'd need two groups of equal sizes, so six in each group.

cues.speaker: RE
cues.text: And how would I tell them apart? I suppose I could put some sort of tag on one group...

cues.speaker: RE
cues.text: or just mark them in some way?

cues.speaker: KE
cues.text: You could use food colouring, that wouldn't hurt them.

cues.speaker: RE
cues.text: Perfect.

cues.speaker: RE
cues.text: Then each group would go into a separate cage, and one group, let's call them group A,

cues.speaker: RE
cues.text: would be the control group. So they'd just have ordinary mouse food.

cues.speaker: RE
cues.text: I suppose you can buy that?

cues.speaker: RE
cues.text: And the other group would have the same as the first group, but they'd also have the

cues.speaker: RE
cues.text: extra sugar.

cues.speaker: RE
cues.text: I might be better to give them something like cereal with it.

cues.speaker: KE
cues.text: Hmm. Then you'd need to weigh the mice, I should think once a week.

cues.speaker: KE
cues.text: And you'd need an electronic balance.

cues.speaker: RE
cues.text: But we can't hold them on the balance, or it'd affect the reading.

cues.speaker: KE
cues.text: Exactly.

cues.speaker: KE
cues.text: So you need something called a weighing chamber to stop the mice from running away.

cues.speaker: KE
cues.text: It sounds complicated, but actually you can just use a plastic box with holes in the top.

cues.speaker: RE
cues.text: OK.

cues.speaker: RE
cues.text: So once we've measured the weight gain of each mouse we can work out the average for each

cues.speaker: RE
cues.text: group, as well as the standard deviation. And then see where we go from there.

cues.speaker: RE
cues.text: That sounds cool, I think the students will enjoy it.
